newsitem.title: UK: New British TV channel wins movie deal with Warner.
newsitem.headline: New British TV channel wins movie deal with Warner.

text.p: British television newcomer Channel 5 is believed to have paid more than 140 million dollars to clinch a major film deal with U.S. film giant Warner Bros, industry sources said on Wednesday.

The deal unveiled on Wednesday covers all Warner Bros feature films released in the United States in 1997 and 1998. It also includes 190 library titles such as box-office hits like as "Batman" and "Driving Miss Daisy" and the classic "Rebel Without A Cause".

Channel 5, a commercial channel launched on March 30, called the deal one of the largest ever involving a British terrestrial TV company. Industry sources said it was thought to have paid more than 140 million dollars to secure the package in the face of competition from the rival ITV commercial network.
Movies are the centrepiece of the Channel 5 schedule, the station running a film in peak time every weekday evening.

"This deal will give 5 many of the upcoming box office hits opening in the next two years, demonstrating the channel's commitment to bringing viewers Hollywood's best," said Dawn Airey, the station's director of programmes.

Channel 5, in which British media groups Pearson Plc and United News & Media Plc are major shareholders, said the investment was on top of its modest core programme budget of 110 million pounds ($180 million) a year.
ITV responded by announcing its own film deal with Universal Studios, owned by Seagram Co. Ltd, the Canadian drinks and entertainment giant.
The deal covers 1996/97 releases such as "Liar, Liar" and "The Nutty Professor", along with older movies such as "Back to the Future" and "Jaws".

ITV said it beat off competition from both the BBC and Channel 5 to do the Universal deal. But Channel 5 said that its Warner Bros package comprised some 250 movies, more than double what ITV was getting from Universal.

Channel 5 is Britain's third advertising-funded terrestrial TV station, after the dominant ITV network and Channel 4, which has a special remit to cater for minority tastes. The two BBC channels are funded by an annual licence fee levy and carry no advertising. ITV said on Tuesday that its share of peaktime viewing rose during Channel 5's first week on air. The new channel has been seen as a direct rival to ITV for the mainstream audience but ITV said that early indications were that smaller stations such as BBC2 and Channel 4 were losing out.
Channel 5 is aiming for an audience share of five percent by the end of the year. ITV, which has a much larger budget than its new rival, has a share of 35 percent, rising to 40 percent in peaktime.
